title: Counting Sort
tagline: No comparisons — just tally each value and pour them out in order. O(n + k).

intuition.analogy: To sort a deck where every card is a number from 0–9, you don't compare cards — you make ten piles, drop each card on its pile, then stack the piles 0,1,2,…,9. The order falls out automatically.
paragraphs: Comparison sorts are bounded by O(n log n) because each comparison only gives one bit of information. Counting sort sidesteps comparisons entirely: if keys are small integers in [0, k], you can use the value itself as an array index.

Step one tallies how many times each value appears. Step two turns those counts into starting positions via a prefix sum. Step three places each element directly where it belongs. Total work is proportional to n (the elements) plus k (the value range).

It shines when k is not much bigger than n (e.g. ages, exam scores, bytes). When k is huge (like 64-bit integers), the count array becomes impractical — that's where radix sort layers counting sort over digits.
intuition.keyIdea: When keys are small integers, the value is its own index — count occurrences and emit in order, skipping comparisons.

steps.title: Find the range
steps.detail: Determine max value M (and optionally min, to shift negatives). Allocate count[0..M].

steps.title: Tally
steps.detail: For each element v, increment count[v]. Now count[v] is how many times v occurs.

steps.title: Prefix sum (for stability)
steps.detail: Convert counts to positions: count[v] += count[v-1] gives the index where the last v should go, enabling a stable placement.

steps.title: Place
steps.detail: Walk the input from right to left, placing each element at its counted position and decrementing the count — preserving original order among equal keys.

code.title: counting_sort.py

complexity.timeReason: One pass to count (n), one pass over the value range to emit (k).
complexity.spaceReason: The count array is size k; the output array is size n.

pitfalls: Fails or wastes huge memory when the value range k is enormous.
Negative numbers need an offset (shift by -min) before indexing.
The simple 'emit by frequency' version is fine for plain integers; you need the prefix-sum version to stay stable when sorting records by a key.

dryRun.clickMoment: There was never a single comparison between two elements. Sorting became 'array indexing', which is why it beats the n log n comparison barrier for small integer keys.

problems.title: Sort an Array
problems.statement: Sort integers within a known small range using counting sort.
problems.hint: Tally then emit; offset if negatives are present.

problems.title: Sort Colors
problems.hint: Counting sort with k=3 is a clean one-liner; or do it in one pass with three pointers.

problems.title: Relative Sort Array
problems.statement: Sort arr1 so elements follow the order in arr2; the rest go ascending at the end.
problems.hint: Counting array indexed by value lets you emit in any prescribed order.
problems.tests: Counting sort with a custom emission order.

problems.title: Maximum Gap
problems.statement: Find the maximum gap between successive elements in sorted order, in linear time.
problems.hint: Bucket/counting ideas give linear-time sorting needed here.

problems.title: H-Index
problems.statement: Compute a researcher's h-index from citation counts.
problems.hint: Bucket citations by count (capped at n), then sweep from high to low accumulating.
